en: Thus have I heard: the Dhammacetiyasutta, the eighty-ninth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Medāḷupa.
Now on that occasion King Pasenadi of Kosala had arrived at Nagaraka for some business or other.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed Dīgha Kārāyaṇa:
“Harness, dear Kārāyaṇa, the finest carriages; let us go to the park grounds to see the beautiful landscape.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” Dīgha Kārāyaṇa replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala. Having harnessed the finest carriages, he informed King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“The finest carriages have been readied for you, Your Majesty.”
"Now, depart whenever you deem it the right time.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala mounted his excellent vehicle and, with his excellent vehicles and in great royal splendor,
set out from the city and proceeded toward the monastery.
Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground was passable for a carriage, he alighted from the carriage and entered the monastery on foot.
As King Pasenadi of Kosala was walking and wandering back and forth for exercise in the monastery,
he saw at the foot of trees places that were serene, inspiring, quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, and suitable for the seclusion of human beings.
suitable for seclusion.
Having seen them, mindfulness arose in him directed toward the Blessed One:
"These indeed are those roots of trees—lovely, inspiring, quiet, free from noise, secluded from people..."
"Secret and secluded places suitable for retreat, where we used to attend upon that Blessed One,
the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed Dīgha Kārāyaṇa:
“Indeed, my dear Kārāyaṇa, these are those delightful and inspiring tree roots—
quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, remote from human habitation, and suitable for seclusion—
where we used to attend upon that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“Where, my dear Kārāyaṇa, does that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwell at present?
“There is, Great King, a Sakyan town named Medāḷupa.
There that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwells at present.”
“But how far away, friend Kārāyaṇa, is the Sakyans’ market town called Medāḷupa from the city?
“It is not far, Great King;
it is three yojanas.”
“It is possible to go with the remainder of the day.
“In that case, dear Kārāyaṇa, have the excellent, fine carriages harnessed; we shall go to see that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
“Yes, Your Majesty,” Dīgha Kārāyaṇa replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala, and having had the excellent, fine carriages harnessed, he informed King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“Your Majesty, your excellent chariots are indeed ready.
Now, do as you deem timely.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala mounted an excellent chariot and, with his excellent chariots, set out from the city toward the Sakyans’ market town named Medāḷupa.
With the remainder of that very day, he arrived at the Sakyan town named Medāḷupa.
He proceeded toward the monastery;
having gone by carriage as far as the ground was passable for a carriage, he alighted from the carriage and entered the monastery on foot.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were walking back and forth in the open air.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached those bhikkhus; having approached, he said this to them:
"Venerable sirs, where is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwelling at present?"
“For we truly desire to see that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
“Great King, this dwelling has its door closed. Approach quietly and without haste; enter the porch, clear your throat, and knock on the bolt. The Blessed One will open the door for you.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala gave his sword and turban right there to Dīgha Kārāyaṇa.
Then it occurred to Dīgha Kārāyaṇa:
“The king is now retiring; I must remain right here.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, approaching that monastery with little noise as its door was closed, entered the porch unhurriedly, coughed, and knocked on the bolt. The Blessed One opened the door.

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala entered the monastery, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name:
"I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir;
I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir."
“But what benefit do you perceive, Great King, that you perform such supreme service toward this body and offer yourself as a sacrifice?
“There is, venerable sir, a logical inference regarding the Blessed One in me:
‘The Blessed One is a perfectly awakened Buddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced the good way.’”
"Here, venerable sir, I see some recluses and brahmins who practice a limited holy life for ten years, twenty years, thirty years, or even forty years;
yet after some time, they become well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beards trimmed, and live indulging themselves, provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure.
But here, venerable sir, I see bhikkhus practicing the holy life completely and purely, unto the end of life, as long as breath lasts."
But indeed, venerable sir, I do not see any other spiritual life outside here that is so complete and pure.
This too, venerable sir, is my inference regarding the Dhamma concerning the Blessed One:
“The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well.”
Furthermore, venerable sir, kings quarrel with kings,
kṣatriyas quarrel with kṣatriyas, brahmins quarrel with brahmins, householders quarrel with householders; even a mother quarrels with her son,
a son quarrels with his mother, a father quarrels with his son, and a son quarrels with his father.
A brother quarrels with his sister, a sister quarrels with her brother, and a companion quarrels with his companion.
But here, venerable sir, I see monks living in harmony, in mutual agreement, without dispute, like milk and water mixed together, looking upon one another with eyes of affection.
Indeed, venerable sir, I do not see any other assembly outside of this one that is so harmonious.
“Venerable sir, this too is my inference regarding the Blessed One:
‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well.
Furthermore, venerable sir, I used to wander and stroll from monastery to monastery and from park to park.”

"There I saw some recluses and brahmins who were emaciated, haggard, discolored, and jaundiced, with veins protruding over their limbs; they seemed, I thought, as if they could hardly bear to be looked at by people.
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to me:
'Surely these venerable ones either lead the holy life without enthusiasm, or they have committed some evil deed that must be concealed.'"
"For indeed, these venerable ones are emaciated, coarse, discolored, jaundiced, with limbs covered in visible veins; they do not seem to catch the eye of people when looked upon.
Having approached them, I said this:
"Why, venerable sirs, are you emaciated, coarse, discolored, jaundiced, with limbs covered in visible veins, as if you do not catch the eye of people when looked upon?"
They said to me thus:
"We have a kinsman’s disease, Great King.

But here, Bhante, I see bhikkhus with uplifted faces, elated and joyful in appearance, their faculties refreshed, free from cares, their hair serene, living on what others give, dwelling with minds like those of deer.
Then, Bhante, this occurred to me:
“Surely these venerable ones perceive a sublime distinction between what was before and what is now in the teaching of that Blessed One;

for indeed, these venerable ones are joyful and exultant, uplifted and exceedingly glad, their faculties refreshed, free from anxiety, with hair standing on end, living on what others give, dwelling with minds like those of deer.”
"Furthermore, venerable sir, I have this inference regarding the Dhamma from the Blessed One:
'The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well.
Moreover, venerable sir, there is a consecrated khattiya king."
"I am capable of having this man executed, or having him fined, or having him banished.
Yet, venerable sir, while I am sitting in the court of justice, they interrupt my speech from time to time.
Thus, I do not obtain [the outcome I desire]."
‘Sirs, do not interrupt my speech while I am seated at the court of justice; sirs, please wait for the conclusion of my discourse.
Yet, venerable sir, they still interrupt my speech from time to time.
But here, venerable sir, I see these monks;
At whatever time the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds, at that time there is neither the sound of spitting nor the sound of coughing among the Blessed One’s disciples.
Once, venerable sir, while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds,
a certain disciple of the Blessed One coughed.
Then a certain fellow celibate nudged me with his knee, saying:
“Venerable sir, be quiet; do not make a noise, Venerable sir; our Blessed Teacher is teaching the Dhamma.
At that, venerable sir, this thought occurred to me:
‘It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
Truly, sir, such a well-disciplined assembly will exist without the use of the rod or the sword.
Yet, venerable sir, I do not see any other assembly outside of this one that is so well-disciplined.”
“Furthermore, venerable sir, I have this inference regarding the Dhamma from the Blessed One:
‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well.

Moreover, venerable sir, I see here certain wise khattiyas, skillful and accomplished in the doctrines of others, who are like those who pierce hair with a needle. They move about as if splitting through the various views with the sword of wisdom.”
They hear:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama will indeed descend upon such-and-such a village or town.
They then formulate a question:
‘We shall approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question.
If he is asked thus, he will answer thus, and we shall refute his argument in such a way;
and if he is asked thus, he will answer thus, and we shall likewise refute his argument.’
They hear:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama has indeed arrived at such-and-such a village or town.
They then approach the Blessed One.
The Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, they did not even ask the Blessed One a question, much less engage in debate;
rather, they simply became his disciples.
“Venerable sir, this too is my inference regarding the Blessed One:
‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.
Furthermore, venerable sir, I see here certain brahmin scholars... [and so forth]”
Householder-scholars... [and so on] ...
ascetic-scholars who are subtle, skilled in the doctrines of others, and like hair-splitting archers. They move about as if piercing through various views with the weapon of wisdom.
They hear:
‘The ascetic Gotama, sirs, will indeed come to such-and-such a village or town.
They then prepare a question, thinking:
‘Having approached the ascetic Gotama, we shall ask him this question.’
‘If he is asked thus, he will answer thus, and we shall refute his position in this way;
and if he is asked thus, he will answer thus, and we shall refute his position in that way.
They hear:
‘The ascetic Gotama has indeed arrived at such-and-such a village or town.
They approach the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One instructs, urges, inspires, and gladdens them with a discourse on the Dhamma.

When they had been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, they did not even ask the Blessed One a question, much less enter into debate; instead,
they simply requested the Blessed One for permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness,
and the Blessed One ordained them.
Having thus gone forth, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, they soon realized for themselves through direct knowledge,
in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness;
having attained it, they dwelt therein.
They said this:
“Alas, sir, we have been deceived! Alas, sir, we have been deceived!
For previously, while not being ascetics, we claimed to be ascetics; while not being brahmins, we claimed to be brahmins; while not being arahants, we claimed to be arahants.”
‘Now we are ascetics; now we are brahmins; now we are arahants.
This too, venerable sir, is my inference regarding the Dhamma from the Blessed One:
‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well.’”
"Furthermore, Bhante, these two chief ministers, Isidatta and Purāṇa, have their food from me and their vehicles from me; I am the provider of their livelihood and the bringer of their fame.
Yet they do not show such deference toward me as they do toward the Blessed One.
Once in the past, Bhante, when I had set out on a military expedition and was testing these two chief ministers, Isidatta and Purāṇa, I took up residence in a certain cramped lodging."

Then, venerable sir, these two chief ministers, Isidatta and Purāṇa, having spent much of the night in talk on the Dhamma, lay down with their heads toward where the Blessed One was and their feet toward me.
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to me:
“How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!”
"These overseers, Isidatta and Purāṇa, are my dependents and my servants; I am their provider of livelihood and bringer of honor.
Yet they do not show such humble reverence toward me as they do toward the Blessed One.
Surely these venerable ones perceive a sublime distinction, superior and more excellent, within the teaching of that Blessed One."
"Venerable sir, this too is my inference regarding the Blessed One:
'The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well.
Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is a kshatriya, and I too am a kshatriya."
The Blessed One is a Kosalan, and I am a Kosalan;
the Blessed One is eighty years old, and I am eighty years old.

Venerable sir, since the Blessed One is a kshatriya and I am a kshatriya, the Blessed One is a Kosalan and I am a Kosalan, and the Blessed One is eighty years old and I am eighty years old; [in these respects we are equal].
“By this, Bhante, I have indeed been able to perform the highest act of homage toward the Blessed One and to offer a tribute of friendship.
Now, Bhante, we depart;
we have many duties and much to do.”
“Now, Great King, you may go at whatever time you deem appropriate.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Not long after King Pasenadi of Kosala had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, King Pasenadi of Kosala has spoken these monuments of Dhamma and, rising from his seat, departed.
Monks, you should learn these monuments of Dhamma;
monks, you should master these monuments of Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, you should preserve the shrines of the Dhamma.
For the shrines of the Dhamma, bhikkhus, are beneficial and pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The ninth discourse, the Dhammacetiyasutta, is finished.
